entries.name: Slate
entries.notes: Splits into flat sheets along slaty cleavage; the classic roofing stone. Purple and green varieties are ornamental.

entries.name: Phyllite
entries.notes: Slate that went further: silky sheen from microscopic mica. Rippled (crenulated) surfaces are a field marker.

entries.name: Mica schist
entries.weathers_to: micaceous sandy soil, quartz sand, clay
entries.notes: Sparkles in sunlight — the easiest metamorphic to recognize. Schistosity is the designer's friend for layered placement.

entries.name: Gneiss
entries.notes: Banded light/dark stripes from high-grade metamorphism. Ancient cores of every continent; often billions of years old.

entries.name: Marble
entries.weathers_to: terra rossa, karst landscape, red clay
entries.notes: Dissolves in rain: karst terrain, sinkholes, caves. Cararra and Carrara-style white marble built Rome.

entries.name: Quartzite
entries.notes: Nearly pure silica; harder than steel tools bite it. Makes the sharpest, most rugged ridgelines in a terrain.

entries.name: Hornfels
entries.notes: Baked by a nearby intrusion; extremely hard, splintery, blocky. Spotted hornfels carries andalusite eyes.

entries.name: Amphibolite
entries.type: regional metamorphic rock (medium to high grade)
entries.notes: Dark, tough, mineral-dark banded when lineated. Superb crushed stone; excellent quarry rock.

entries.name: Greenschist
entries.notes: The first step up from basalt/sea-floor alteration. The whole greenschist facies defines low-grade metamorphism worldwide.

entries.name: Greenstone
entries.notes: Ancient metamorphosed lava; the classic host of Archean gold (Pilbara, Superior, Kaapvaal). Feels dense and green in the hand.

entries.name: Blueschist
entries.notes: The fingerprint of a cold subduction zone — blue amphibole needles. Rare at the surface; every occurrence is a fossil trench.

entries.name: Eclogite
entries.notes: Forms deeper than 30 km and can be denser than the mantle it sits in. Red garnet studded in dark green pyroxene.

entries.name: Granulite
entries.notes: Baked dry and bone-hard, no mica left; the deepest common crustal rock. Large provinces surface in southern India and Sri Lanka.

entries.name: Charnockite
entries.notes: Named after the tomb slab of Job Charnock in St John's, Kolkata. A Madras-black building stone of South Asia.

entries.name: Migmatite
entries.notes: Not quite magma, not quite rock: swirling light veins through dark country rock. Maps beautifully onto banded textures.

entries.name: Skarn
uses: ore host (copper, tungsten, zinc, iron, gold)
entries.notes: Where granite bakes limestone, metals concentrate: world-class Cu-W-Zn skarn deposits. Rust-red, green or brown, coarse and sparkly.

entries.name: Calc-silicate rock
entries.notes: The impure cousin of marble: green, banded, sparkly. A useful marker of original silty limestone protoliths.

entries.name: Serpentinite
entries.notes: Greasy, green, mottled; grows strange plants because of the toxic magnesium soil. Fault zones on serpentinite can host asbestos fibers.

entries.name: Soapstone
entries.notes: Soft enough to scratch with a fingernail; carved for millennia into figures, molds, stoves. An industrial talc ore.

entries.name: Mylonite
entries.notes: Rock milled to flour by kilometre-scale shearing, then recrystallized; ribbons of stretched grains record the direction of the fault.

entries.name: Phyllonite
entries.notes: A schist milled so fine it greasy-shines like phyllite. Marks the deepest roots of big faults.

entries.name: Cataclasite
made_of: broken angular fragments in fine matrix
entries.notes: Rock crushed brittlely near the surface; hardness and look depend entirely on the parent rock. A fault 'scar' you can walk on.

entries.name: Pseudotachylite
entries.notes: Friction from a giant earthquake melted the fault surface; it quenched to black glass veins. The fossil of a single slip event.

entries.name: Metaconglomerate
entries.notes: Pebbles flattened and stretched into almond shapes — augen conglomerate. Fossil riverbeds with the pebbles blurred like smeared paint.

entries.name: Metagreywacke
entries.notes: The backbone of New Zealand's Southern Alps (Rakaia terrane). Turbidite layers record deep-sea fan deposits, metamorphosed in the trench.

entries.name: Anthracite
entries.notes: Coal cooked into near-pure carbon: hard, lustrous, smokeless, highest heat of any coal. The end of the line for metamorphosed organics.

entries.name: Jadeitite (jadeite rock)
entries.weathers_to: fine silt; resistant boulders in river terraces
entries.notes: World's premier jade: apple-green boulders in gravel terraces, mined since antiquity. Imperial jade is translucent emerald green.

entries.name: Nephrite (jade)
entries.notes: Tough, waxy, felted fibres; worked by Māori and Chinese for 8,000 years. New Zealand greenstone adzes came from South Island rivers.

entries.name: Itabirite
entries.notes: The principal iron ore of Brazil — banded hematite-quartz rock, named for Itabira. Hosts world-class reserves; dense, rust-red, heavy in the hand.

entries.name: Garnet schist
entries.type: regional metamorphic rock (medium to high grade)
entries.notes: Wine-red garnets studded across glittering mica; the workhorse index mineral for medium-grade metamorphism.

entries.name: Kyanite schist
entries.notes: Kyanite is anisotropic: scratches like 5.5 along the blade, like 7 across it. Mined for high-temperature refractories.

entries.name: Graphitic schist
entries.notes: Ancient plankton cooked to pure carbon seams; Sri Lankan crystalline graphite is the world's purest natural graphite.

entries.name: Augen gneiss
entries.notes: Eye-shaped feldspar porphyroblasts floating in the banding; 'Augen' is German for eyes. Ornamental and unmistakable.

entries.name: Leptite
entries.notes: Pale, fine-grained, ancient felsic volcanics metamorphosed alongside Bergslagen's iron and base-metal ores.

entries.name: Khondalite
entries.notes: A garnet-sillimanite gneiss of the Eastern Ghats; sillimanite here feeds India's refractory industry.

entries.name: Coticule (Belgian yellow whetstone)
entries.notes: Prized razor stone: releases slurry of ultrafine spessartine grains under water, polishing edges to a mirror. Quarried continuously since the 1500s.
